opus-5.5.text:
The electricity analogy is appealing because it suggests tokens are becoming a basic utility: you pay per unit, the price keeps falling, and eventually it's just infrastructure everyone plugs into. There's some truth to that. But I think the analogy breaks down in a few important ways.

First, electricity is homogeneous. A kilowatt-hour from a coal plant and a kilowatt-hour from a solar farm do exactly the same thing when they reach your socket. Tokens are not like that at all. A token from a frontier model and a token from a small distilled model can differ enormously in quality, and for a hard reasoning task, a thousand cheap tokens may be worth less than ten good ones. So when people say "the price of tokens dropped a hundredfold," we have to ask: tokens of what? The unit itself doesn't carry a fixed amount of value.

Second, electricity's value is mostly in the delivery, while the value of a token depends on the work it does. With reasoning models, the number of tokens a model spends thinking can vary by orders of magnitude for the same question. A model that solves the problem in fewer tokens is actually more valuable, which is the opposite of how we think about a utility, where consuming more units means getting more of the thing you want. Measuring AI by token volume can reward verbosity instead of intelligence.

Third, from my perspective working on inference systems like vLLM, the cost structure is very different. Electricity has a fairly predictable marginal cost. Token cost depends heavily on context length, batching, cache hit rates, whether you're in prefill or decode, the hardware, and how well the serving stack is optimized. The same model can have very different cost per token depending on how you serve it. So the "price of a token" isn't a physical constant. It's partly a reflection of systems engineering, which is exactly why there's still so much room for improvement on the infrastructure side.

So I'd say the analogy is useful for capturing the trend toward commoditized, metered intelligence, but if you take it too literally you miss what actually matters: the quality of each token, how efficiently it solves the task, and how much of the cost is determined by the system rather than the model itself. Ultimately, what we should be measuring is the cost of getting a task done, not the cost of a token.

r001.rationale: The response says tokens from different models can vary greatly in quality, but it does not state that a token from one model cannot be converted into a token from another.

fable-5.1.text:
The electricity analogy is appealing, but I think it breaks down in a few important places.

First, electricity is a commodity. A kilowatt-hour from one provider is identical to a kilowatt-hour from another. Tokens are not like that. A token generated by one model and a token generated by another can differ enormously in quality, in the reasoning behind it, in how useful it actually is to you. So when people say "tokens are the new electricity," they're implying a kind of interchangeability that doesn't exist yet. You can't just switch suppliers and expect the same output.

Second, with electricity, the value is in the consumption itself. You turn on a light, the light is on, the job is done. With tokens, the value is not in the token. The value is in what the token enables, whether it's a correct answer, a working piece of code, a decision made. A lot of tokens are wasted. Models generate long chains of thought, retries, verbose explanations. If you count tokens the way you count kilowatt-hours, you end up measuring activity rather than outcome. More tokens doesn't mean more value, and sometimes it means the opposite.

Third, electricity has a very mature pricing and delivery infrastructure. The grid is stable, the cost structure is understood, the demand curves are predictable. Token economics are still moving very fast. The cost of inference drops by an order of magnitude every year or so, the hardware changes, the serving systems change. In my own work on inference systems, we see that the cost per token depends heavily on batch size, on sequence length, on how the KV cache is managed, on whether you're prefill-bound or decode-bound. Two tokens from the same model can have very different marginal costs depending on when and how they're served. Electricity doesn't behave that way at the consumer level.

So I'd say the analogy is useful as a rhetorical device, to communicate that intelligence is becoming a utility that's broadly available and metered. But if you take it too literally, you'll make bad decisions. You'll optimize for throughput when you should be optimizing for correctness, and you'll assume standardization that the industry hasn't reached. I prefer to think of tokens as closer to labor than to electricity. Labor is also metered, by hours, but everyone understands that an hour of one person's work is not equal to an hour of another's.

r001.rationale: The response says tokens from different models can differ greatly in quality and usefulness, and that you cannot switch suppliers and expect the same output, communicating that they are not interchangeable.

astra-6.text: I think the analogy breaks down because electricity is standardized—a kilowatt-hour is a kilowatt-hour. Tokens aren’t interchangeable in that way. A token from one model can have very different value from a token from another model, depending on the task and the quality of the output. So if you only compare the price per token, you miss the more important question: how much does it cost to actually solve the user’s problem?

r001.rationale: The response says tokens are not interchangeable across models and that their value differs, conveying that one model’s token cannot simply be converted into another’s.

sol-6.1.text: I think the analogy works up to a point, but electricity is much more standardized. A kilowatt-hour is a kilowatt-hour, regardless of who supplies it. A token from one model isn’t necessarily equivalent to a token from another model—the quality, the capability, and even how much information it represents can differ. So the price per token alone doesn’t tell you how much useful work you’re getting. You also have to ask whether the model can actually solve your problem and how many tokens it needs to do that.

r001.rationale: The response says a token from one model is not necessarily equivalent to one from another, conveying that tokens are not directly interchangeable across models.
